teaching.h: Why every noun has a gender
teaching.p: Spanish nouns are masculine or feminine, and the article (el/la) has to match. The good news: endings are a strong clue — most -o words are masculine, most -a words are feminine — but it's not 100%, so the article gets learned together with the noun, like in German.
teaching.exTranslation: the book (m), the table (f)

teaching.h: The four definite articles
teaching.p: One word for 'the' becomes four in Spanish, split by gender AND number.
teaching.ex: el gato, la casa, los gatos, las casas
teaching.exTranslation: the cat, the house, the cats, the houses

teaching.h: Indefinite articles work the same way
teaching.p: un for masculine, una for feminine — the 'a/an' equivalent.
teaching.exTranslation: a dog, a flower

teaching.h: The exceptions everyone learns the hard way
teaching.p: A handful of common words break the -o/-a pattern. 'día' (day) looks feminine but is masculine; 'mano' (hand) looks masculine but is feminine. These get memorized individually.
teaching.exTranslation: the day, the hand

quiz.q: ___ perro es grande. (the dog is big)
Which of these is an exception (masculine despite -a ending)?
Tengo ___ flor bonita. (I have a pretty flower)
The plural feminine definite article is:

teaching.h: Why Spanish needs two different verbs for 'to be'
teaching.p: English uses one word for both permanent identity and temporary states, which hides a real distinction. Spanish makes it explicit: ser for what something fundamentally IS, estar for the state it's currently IN.
teaching.exTranslation: She is a doctor. I am tired.

teaching.h: Ser: identity, traits, origin, profession
teaching.p: Things that don't change moment to moment.
teaching.exTranslation: She is a doctor.

teaching.h: Estar: feelings, conditions, location
teaching.p: Things that can change today, tomorrow, or in five minutes.
teaching.exTranslation: I am tired.

teaching.h: The same adjective, two different meanings
teaching.p: This is the clearest proof the distinction is real: swapping ser/estar with the identical adjective genuinely changes what you're saying.
teaching.ex: Él es aburrido. Él está aburrido.
teaching.exTranslation: He is boring (a trait). He is bored (right now).

teaching.h: Location always uses estar — even permanently
teaching.p: This one surprises learners: you'd think a city's location is permanent, so it 'should' be ser — but Spanish always uses estar for location, no exceptions.
teaching.exTranslation: Madrid is in Spain.

quiz.q: Which verb is used for profession?
Madrid ___ en España. (is in Spain — estar)
Which verb is used for temporary feelings?

teaching.h: Three verb families, one pattern each
teaching.p: Every Spanish verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir, and each family conjugates in its own consistent way. Learn the pattern once per family, and you can conjugate hundreds of regular verbs.
teaching.exTranslation: to speak, to eat, to live

teaching.h: -ar verbs
teaching.p: The most common family.
teaching.ex: hablar → hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, habláis, hablan
teaching.exTranslation: to speak → I speak, you speak, he/she speaks, we speak, you all speak, they speak

teaching.h: -er verbs
teaching.p: Very similar to -ar, with e instead of a in most endings.
teaching.ex: comer → como, comes, come, comemos, coméis, comen
teaching.exTranslation: to eat → I eat, you eat, he/she eats, we eat, you all eat, they eat

teaching.h: -ir verbs
teaching.p: Nearly identical to -er, differing only in the nosotros/vosotros forms.
teaching.ex: vivir → vivo, vives, vive, vivimos, vivís, viven
teaching.exTranslation: to live → I live, you live, he/she lives, we live, you all live, they live

teaching.h: Regular endings across all three families, side by side
teaching.p: Once you see -ar, -er, and -ir stacked together, the pattern is obvious: swap the vowel, keep the same skeleton. hablar (to speak), comer (to eat), and vivir (to live) as the model verbs.

teaching.h: Subject pronouns — often skipped entirely
teaching.p: Because Spanish verb endings already show who's doing the action, subject pronouns (yo, tú...) are frequently dropped altogether — 'hablo' alone already means 'I speak', pronoun optional.
teaching.exTranslation: I speak. We speak.

teaching.h: Direct object pronouns replace the thing being acted on
teaching.p: Once something's already been mentioned, these pronouns let you avoid repeating the full noun.
teaching.exTranslation: I see it/him.

teaching.h: Indirect object pronouns answer 'to/for whom?'
teaching.p: Different set of pronouns for the receiver of an action, as opposed to the thing directly acted on.
teaching.exTranslation: I give him/her the book.

teaching.h: Placement: before the conjugated verb
teaching.p: Unlike English, where object pronouns come after the verb, Spanish usually places them right before it.
teaching.exTranslation: I love you.

quiz.q: The indirect object pronoun for "to him/her" is:

teaching.h: Two pasts because Spanish separates 'event' from 'background'
teaching.p: This mirrors ser/estar's logic: one tense for a specific completed action, another for the ongoing backdrop it happened against.
teaching.ex: Comí pizza ayer. Cuando era niño, jugaba fútbol.
teaching.exTranslation: I ate pizza yesterday. When I was a child, I used to play soccer.

teaching.h: Preterite — a finished, specific event
teaching.p: Use this for something that happened and ended at a definite point.
teaching.exTranslation: I ate pizza yesterday.

teaching.h: Imperfect — descriptions, habits, ongoing background
teaching.p: Use this for 'used to' situations, ongoing states, or scene-setting — not a single finished event.
teaching.exTranslation: When I was a child, I used to play soccer.

teaching.h: Preterite conjugation pattern (-ar)
teaching.ex: hablar → hablé, hablaste, habló, hablamos, hablasteis, hablaron
teaching.exTranslation: I spoke, you spoke, he/she spoke, we spoke, you all spoke, they spoke

teaching.h: Imperfect conjugation pattern (-ar)
teaching.ex: hablar → hablaba, hablabas, hablaba, hablábamos, hablabais, hablaban
teaching.exTranslation: I used to speak, you used to speak, he/she used to speak, we used to speak, you all used to speak, they used to speak

quiz.q: Cuando era niño, ___ fútbol. (I used to play — jugar, imperfect)
Which tense describes background/description in the past?

teaching.h: Why part of speech matters extra in Spanish
teaching.p: Because Spanish adjectives agree with the nouns they describe, correctly identifying a word's category is what tells you whether it needs to match gender/number at all.
teaching.exTranslation: to run (verb), fast (adverb), teacher (noun)

teaching.h: Sustantivos and pronombres work together
teaching.p: Same relationship as in English — pronouns exist so you don't repeat the same noun endlessly.
teaching.ex: La maestra calificó los exámenes. Ella estaba cansada.
teaching.exTranslation: The teacher graded the exams. She was tired.

teaching.h: Verbos drive the action; adjetivos describe and must agree
teaching.p: Unlike English adjectives, Spanish ones change ending to match the noun's gender and number — 'alta' here matches 'maestra' being feminine.
teaching.ex: La maestra alta corre cada mañana.
teaching.exTranslation: The tall teacher runs every morning.

teaching.h: Preposiciones and conjunciones connect, without carrying standalone meaning
teaching.ex: El gato está sobre la mesa, pero duerme.
teaching.exTranslation: The cat is on the table, but it's sleeping.

quiz.q: In "Corre rápido," what part of speech is "rápido"?
Which word is a preposición in "El gato está sobre la mesa"?
Él es un ___ maestro. (a good teacher — bueno/buen)
Which word class joins two clauses, like "y" or "porque"?

teaching.h: Oración simple — one complete idea
teaching.exTranslation: The dog barked.

teaching.h: Oración compuesta — two equal ideas joined
teaching.p: Connected with y, pero, or o — each half could be its own sentence.
teaching.ex: El perro ladró, y el gato huyó.
teaching.exTranslation: The dog barked, and the cat ran away.

teaching.h: Oración compleja — one idea depends on another
teaching.ex: Porque llovía, nos quedamos en casa.
teaching.exTranslation: Because it was raining, we stayed home.

teaching.h: Cláusulas subordinadas — the dependent piece
teaching.p: Introduced by porque, cuando, si, que — grammatically incomplete without the main clause.
teaching.exTranslation: ...when he/she arrived home.

quiz.q: "Porque llovía, nos quedamos en casa." is a(n):
El perro ladró, ___ el gato huyó. (and)

teaching.h: Why Spanish has a whole separate mood for uncertainty
teaching.p: The subjunctive exists to grammatically flag 'this isn't a fact, it's a wish, doubt, or emotion.' English does this too in small ways ('I wish I were...'), but Spanish uses it constantly and systematically.
teaching.exTranslation: I hope you come.

teaching.h: Building it from the yo-form
teaching.p: Take the yo-form of the present indicative, drop the -o, then add the OPPOSITE set of endings (-ar verbs get e-endings, -er/-ir verbs get a-endings).
teaching.exTranslation: (that) I speak, (that) I eat

teaching.h: The trigger phrases that force subjunctive
teaching.p: Certain expressions of hope, necessity, or desire automatically pull the following verb into subjunctive.
teaching.exTranslation: It's important that you study.

teaching.h: Certainty stays indicative — this is the real contrast
teaching.p: When you're simply stating a known fact, use the normal indicative; switch to subjunctive only when there's genuine doubt, wish, or emotion involved.
teaching.ex: Sé que vienes. (indicative) vs. Espero que vengas. (subjunctive)
teaching.exTranslation: I know you're coming. vs. I hope you come.

quiz.q: Espero que ___. (I hope you come — venir, tú, subjunctive)
Es importante que ___. (that you study — estudiar, tú, subjunctive)
"Sé que vienes" uses which mood, and why?

teaching.h: Simple future — one clean pattern
teaching.p: Unlike present tense (which varies by verb family), the future uses the SAME endings for -ar, -er, and -ir verbs alike, attached to the full infinitive.
teaching.exTranslation: I will speak, you will speak, he/she will speak

teaching.h: ir a + infinitive — how people actually talk about the near future
teaching.p: Just like English 'going to', this is the more casual, common way to express near-future plans in everyday speech.
teaching.exTranslation: I'm going to study tomorrow.

teaching.h: Conditional — the Spanish 'would'
teaching.p: Same infinitive-based pattern as the future, but with different endings.
teaching.exTranslation: I would talk to her.

teaching.h: Irregular stems — shared between future and conditional
teaching.p: A handful of common verbs use a shortened, irregular stem for BOTH future and conditional — learn the stem once, apply it to both tenses.
teaching.exTranslation: to have → I will have, I would have

quiz.q: Yo ___ mañana. (I will speak — hablar, simple future)
Yo ___ con ella. (I would talk — hablar, conditional)
The conditional is used to express:
yo ___ (I will have — tener, future, irregular stem)

teaching.h: Real conditions — plain present tense doing the job
teaching.p: For realistic situations, si (if) just pairs with normal present/future tense — no special mood required, same logic as English's first conditional.
teaching.ex: Si llueve, me quedo en casa.
teaching.exTranslation: If it rains, I stay home.

teaching.h: Hypothetical conditions — where subjunctive comes back
teaching.p: For unreal or unlikely situations, si pairs with the imperfect subjunctive, and the result clause uses the conditional.
teaching.exTranslation: If I had money, I would travel.

teaching.h: Imperfect subjunctive formation
teaching.p: Usually built from the preterite ellos-form, swapping the ending for -ra.
teaching.exTranslation: (if I) had, (if I) spoke

teaching.h: Past hypotheticals — imagining a different past
teaching.p: Same idea as third conditional in English: si + pluperfect subjunctive, result in conditional perfect.
teaching.exTranslation: If I had studied, I would have passed.

quiz.q: "Si llueve, me quedo en casa." describes:
Si ___ dinero, viajaría. (if I had money — tener, imperfect subjunctive)
Si hubiera estudiado, ___ aprobado. (I would have passed — haber, conditional perfect)

options: an imagined outcome of the unchangeable past
quiz.answer: an imagined outcome of the unchangeable past

teaching.h: Frase — a chunk with no subject-verb pairing
teaching.exTranslation: in the morning, very fast

teaching.h: Cláusula — has its own subject and verb
teaching.exTranslation: she runs, because he arrived late

teaching.h: Cláusula independiente stands alone
teaching.exTranslation: She runs every morning.

teaching.h: Cláusula dependiente needs the main clause
teaching.p: Has the subject-verb pairing, but the connector word makes it incomplete alone.
teaching.exTranslation: because he arrived late

quiz.q: "por la mañana" is an example of a:
"ella corre" is an example of a:

options: a cláusula has a subject and verb, a frase doesn't
quiz.answer: a cláusula has a subject and verb, a frase doesn't

teaching.h: Voz activa — the default
teaching.exTranslation: The chef cooked the food.

teaching.h: Voz pasiva con ser — formal, less common in speech
teaching.p: ser + past participle + por, structurally similar to English passive but used more sparingly in everyday Spanish.
teaching.ex: La comida fue cocinada por el chef.
teaching.exTranslation: The food was cooked by the chef.

teaching.h: Pasiva refleja — how Spanish speakers actually express this
teaching.p: Using se plus the verb is the far more natural, common way to express passive-like meaning in real conversation.
teaching.exTranslation: Many books were sold.

teaching.h: When passive meaning gets used at all
teaching.p: Same logic as English: when the doer is unknown or unimportant.
teaching.exTranslation: The window broke/was broken.

quiz.q: La comida ___ cocinada por el chef. (was cooked — ser, past)
"Se vendieron muchos libros" is an example of:
___ rompió la ventana. (the window broke — se, pasiva refleja)

teaching.h: Estilo directo — the exact words
teaching.exTranslation: She said: "I am tired."

teaching.h: Estilo indirecto — reporting, with a tense shift
teaching.p: Same backshift logic as English — the reported tense usually moves one step further into the past.
teaching.exTranslation: She said that she was tired.

teaching.h: Present becomes imperfect when reported
teaching.exTranslation: "I am tired" → she said that she was tired

teaching.h: Time words shift to match the new perspective
teaching.p: "hoy" (today) often becomes "ese día" (that day), just like English's today→that day.
teaching.ex: "Vendré hoy" → dijo que vendría ese día
teaching.exTranslation: "I will come today" → she said she would come that day

quiz.q: Ella dijo que ___ cansada. (she was tired — estar, imperfect)
In reported speech, present tense usually shifts to:
"Vendré hoy" reported becomes: dijo que ___ ese día. (venir, conditional)

options: no quotation marks, tense often shifted
quiz.answer: no quotation marks, tense often shifted

teaching.h: Inverted marks — a genuinely unique Spanish feature
teaching.p: ¿ and ¡ appear at the START of questions and exclamations too, not just the end — this actually helps readers, since you know from the first word how to read the intonation.
teaching.exTranslation: How are you? How great!

teaching.h: Capitalization is less frequent than English
teaching.p: Days, months, and nationalities are lowercase in Spanish, unlike English — this trips up a lot of English-speaking learners who over-capitalize by habit.
teaching.exTranslation: Monday, January, Spanish

teaching.h: Commas in lists
teaching.p: Basically the same rule as English.
teaching.exTranslation: I bought apples, bread, and milk.

teaching.h: Accent marks aren't decorative — they change meaning
teaching.p: This is a genuine trap for learners typing quickly: dropping the accent can turn one word into a completely different one.
teaching.ex: tú (you) vs. tu (your), sí (yes) vs. si (if)
teaching.exTranslation: you vs. your, yes vs. if

options: ¿ at the start and ? at the end
quiz.answer: ¿ at the start and ? at the end

quiz.q: In Spanish, days of the week are:

teaching.h: Reflexive verbs — actions directed back at the subject
teaching.p: Similar concept to German's reflexives — a pronoun signals the action loops back to whoever's doing it.
teaching.exTranslation: I get (myself) up. He/she showers (themself).

teaching.h: Por vs. para — the classic learner confusion
teaching.p: Both can translate to English 'for', which is exactly why they're confusing. Rough guide: por = cause, means, duration, movement through; para = purpose, destination, deadline, recipient.
teaching.ex: Camino por el parque. Este regalo es para ti.
teaching.exTranslation: I walk through the park. This gift is for you.

teaching.h: The gerund — for ongoing actions
teaching.p: estar + gerundio mirrors English's continuous tenses closely.
teaching.exTranslation: I am eating. It is raining.

teaching.h: Relative clauses with que/quien
teaching.p: que covers both people and things in most cases; quien is reserved specifically for people, usually after a preposition.
teaching.ex: La mujer que llamó es mi profesora.
teaching.exTranslation: The woman who called is my teacher.

quiz.q: Me ___. (I get up — levantar, reflexive, yo)
La mujer ___ llamó es mi profesora. (relative pronoun)

teaching.h: Why conectores make Spanish sound fluent
teaching.p: Same principle as English — these words explicitly show how ideas relate, turning a list of facts into flowing speech or writing.
teaching.ex: sin embargo, por lo tanto, además, por ejemplo
teaching.exTranslation: however, therefore, furthermore, for example

teaching.h: Showing contrast
teaching.ex: Estaba cansada. Sin embargo, siguió trabajando.
teaching.exTranslation: She was tired. However, she kept working.

teaching.h: Showing cause and result
teaching.ex: Llovió mucho. Por eso, cancelaron el partido.
teaching.exTranslation: It rained a lot. Because of that, they cancelled the game.

teaching.h: Adding ideas
teaching.ex: Es inteligente. Además, es muy trabajadora.
teaching.exTranslation: She's smart. Furthermore, she's very hardworking.

quiz.q: Llovió mucho. ___, cancelaron el partido. (because of that)
